nameStory: False daisy gets its name because it looks like a tiny white daisy at first glance, but it's actually quite different from true daisies. While real daisies are often large and showy, this little imposter stays small and humble, hugging the ground with flowers barely bigger than a pencil eraser.
description: False daisy is a low-growing annual plant that spreads along the ground, reaching up to about 2-3 feet tall but often staying much shorter. It has small white flower heads that look like miniature daisies, each only about a quarter-inch across. The plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in pairs along purplish stems covered in fine white hairs, giving it a somewhat fuzzy appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flower heads only 6-8mm across (about the size of a pencil eraser) with white petals around a yellow center, appearing singly rather than in clusters

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves 2-5 inches long arranged in opposite pairs, with serrated edges and a rough, hairy texture on both sides

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that spreads horizontally along the ground, rarely getting taller than 2-3 feet and often much shorter

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Round, solid stems with a purplish tinge covered in fine white hairs that give them a soft, fuzzy feel

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, bumpy, flattened seeds with narrow wings that feel rough to the touch

habitat: Look for false daisy in wet, muddy areas like the edges of ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams. It thrives in disturbed, moist soils and can often be found along riverbanks or in seasonal flood zones. This plant loves areas that stay consistently damp and can tolerate some salt, so you might spot it in brackish marshes near the coast.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their characteristic opposite leaves becoming visible in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with tiny white flowers appearing throughout the summer months. Plants spread and mat along the ground during this season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, producing seeds that will overwinter in the soil. Plants begin to decline as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following year.

funFact: Despite being called 'false daisy,' this little plant is actually used in traditional medicine around the world and is considered so valuable in some cultures that it's called 'king of hair' because people believe it can prevent hair loss and even turn gray hair black again!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small white asters or true daisies, but false daisy's flowers are much smaller (pencil eraser size) and it grows flat along the ground rather than upright. The opposite leaf arrangement also sets it apart from most asters, which have alternate leaves.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'false daisy' reflects how this plant mimics the appearance of true daisies but belongs to a different group within the sunflower family. While it looks delicate, it's actually quite tough and can grow in conditions too harsh for many other flowering plants.
compareHints: False daisy is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other small white flowers in the sunflower family, it stands out for its ground-hugging growth habit, tiny flower size, and preference for consistently wet conditions. Most similar species either grow taller, have larger flowers, or prefer drier soils.
